summary: The result group gives a k = 10 example for a question Grünbaum posed in print (Math. Intelligencer 2010), where he wrote that no information was available for k ≥ 10. It adds a classification by exact computation of the face-to-face lattice tilers in class C(6) that are unions of golden rhombohedra. This plausibly warrants a research note, and it has a clear specialist audience in discrete geometry: parallelohedra, nonconvex space-fillers, and golden-rhombohedron and quasicrystal polyhedra. The literature account quotes Grünbaum accurately and is candid about the earlier web example, the unread Senechal–Taylor paper and the private correspondence. However, it dates the earliest known solid of this family to Inchbald's page (by March 2023). The same dimpled triacontahedron was published in 2016 by David Hall as a space-filling polyhedron.

findings.message: The literature account names G. Inchbald's web page (dimpling text present by March 2023) as the earlier k = 10 example of this family. An earlier public source exists and is not cited. David Hall's models 'Dimpled Rhombic Triacontahedron - Construction' (Sketchfab, 28 June 2016) and 'DRT with Positive Tetrahedral Translation' (11 July 2016) describe the rhombic triacontahedron with 'one golden rhombohedron [removed] from each of four vertices having tetrahedral symmetry'. They call it 'a delightful new space filling polyhedron' that packs as a lattice and note that it is chiral. This appears to be the solid the account attributes to Inchbald. J. Kostick's vZome pages (April 2022) also show tetrahedrally dimpled triacontahedron arrays. None of these sources mentions zones or Grünbaum's question, and none gives a proof, so the entry's claim (a machine-checked example and a classification) still stands. But the public account of who first exhibited a solid of this family as a space-filler should cite the 2016 source, compare it with Inchbald's solid (same or mirror image), and change the dating 'published on the web before the submitter's work, by March 2023' to match.

internal_notes.message: Checked against the source: the open problem 'Given an even integer k ≥ 4, is there a rhombic monohedral parallelohedron such that every zone has exactly k faces?', the sentence 'No information is available for any k ≥ 10', D1 and D2 as double indentations of Fedorov's rhombic icosahedron (k = 8), and 'None of the other isozonohedra obtainable by indentation of F or T seem to be parallelohedra.' The quotations are accurate. Grünbaum's tentative remark on indentations of T is contradicted by the dimpled triacontahedron (Hall 2016) and by GET A/B. The account could say so explicitly.

Positive evidence for notability: the question was posed explicitly by a leading discrete geometer, and the published record stood at 'no information' for k ≥ 10. The entry gives a rigorous, kernel-checked witness with calibrated definitions, plus a structural classification for C(6) and C(5) (three lemmas, an exhaustive enumeration, and the explanation of the 16-cell pattern). Credible audience: researchers on parallelohedra and space-filling polyhedra (e.g. the Senechal–Taylor line of work, Venkov–McMullen belt theory) and on golden-rhombohedron and quasicrystal polyhedra. Because a solid of this family has been publicly known as a space-filler since 2016, the existential statement alone is less novel than the account suggests. Its value lies in linking the solid to Grünbaum's question, in the proof, and in the classification. Novelty is not required, and this still clears the floor as a plausible research note. The classification is not formalized; it is disclosed honestly as exact computation outside Lean, with undecided cases reported.

The closed-access paper is disclosed as unread, and the abstract was checked. The correspondence is disclosed as unverifiable, and no priority is claimed from it, which fits the policy. Not a finding.

It shows several dimpled triacontahedron variants (octahedral, tetrahedral, 3-fold axis, z-axis dimples), mostly in mixed arrays with convex triacontahedra. I could not tell whether any single-tile array matches GET A or GET B. The tetrahedral array is probably the Hall/Inchbald solid. Worth a check by the submitter and a mention in the account.
It has 54 faces, so it is not a 30-face member of class C(6). It is a related triacontahedron-derived space-filler and could be mentioned. Its page body did not load.

The submitter states that no systematic search of other proof libraries was made. I found no Lean, Isabelle or Coq formalization of parallelohedra or polyhedron zones in the searches above. This is a minor gap only.
Disclosed as not read. Grünbaum cites it for an eightfold indentation of T. Not material to k = 10.

what_would_reach_higher: Cite David Hall's Sketchfab models (28 June and 11 July 2016) as the earliest known public description of the four-dimple (tetrahedral) triacontahedron as a lattice space-filler. Change the account's dating of the earlier example and its Inchbald-first framing to match.

State whether Hall's chiral DRT is congruent (or mirror-congruent) to Inchbald's solid, using the same exact congruence check over the 120 star symmetries used for GET A and GET B. Say explicitly that neither GET A nor GET B appears in Hall's or Kostick's pages.
Check J. Kostick's vZome arrays (2022) and S. Kabai's 54-faced space-filler, and record them in the sources-checked list with a one-line comparison each.

Note explicitly that these solids contradict Grünbaum's tentative remark that no other indentations of T seem to be parallelohedra (already contradicted by the 2016 solid), and present the contribution as linking these solids to his zone question, proving the example and classifying C(6).
Formalize the C(6) classification theorem (or at least the 16-cell count) in Lean, so that the stronger structural result is part of the checked statement rather than the informal account.
Run and record a search of other proof libraries (Isabelle AFP, Coq/Rocq, HOL Light) for parallelohedra and zone formalizations.
If a free route opens (author copy, institutional repository), read Senechal–Taylor 2023 in full and state which Grünbaum statement it counters and how its three solids differ from GET A and GET B.
